# The Lantern That Would Not Die

In the autumn of the third year of Emperor Wudi's reign, there lived a magistrate named Chen Weiming in the remote district of Qinghe. He was known as a just man, though perhaps too proud of his own virtue.

One evening, as Chen walked the empty corridors of the yamen after all servants had retired, he noticed a faint glow emanating from the Hall of Records. Thinking a clerk had left a lantern burning—a waste of oil and a fire risk—he went to extinguish it.

Inside, he found an old woman sitting at the records table, her face illuminated by a single paper lantern. She wore burial clothes, white as bone, and her fingers traced along an open ledger.

"Old mother," Chen said, his voice steady despite the cold that crept into his chest, "the yamen is closed. How did you enter?"

The woman did not look up. "I have been here longer than you, Magistrate. Longer than your father's father walked this earth."

Chen stepped closer and saw that the ledger she touched was from sixty years past—a case file, yellowed and crumbling.

"I am looking for my name," she said. "When I find it, I may rest."

---

The old woman told her story in a voice like dry leaves scraping stone.

She had been a widow named Madame Hu, accused of poisoning her wealthy brother-in-law to steal his estate. The magistrate of that time—a man who had accepted bribes from the true culprit, the brother-in-law's own son—had sentenced her to death by slow slicing. She had died over three days, proclaiming her innocence with every breath until she had no breath left.

"The true record was altered," she whispered. "Somewhere in these halls, the original testimony exists. The clerk who wrote the truth hid it, too frightened to speak but too honorable to destroy it completely."

Chen felt his pride stir. Here was an injustice he could correct.

"I will find it," he declared. "I will restore your honor."

The old woman finally raised her face. Where her eyes should have been were only shadows, deep and endless.

"Many magistrates have made that promise," she said. "They search for a night, perhaps two. Then they convince themselves I am merely a dream, a trick of exhaustion. They forget. They always forget."

---

Chen did not forget.

For seven nights, he searched the Hall of Records, the storage rooms, the spaces behind walls where old documents had been stuffed and abandoned. His servants whispered that the magistrate had gone mad, spending his nights talking to shadows, refusing sleep.

On the eighth night, behind a loose brick in the oldest part of the building, Chen found a bamboo scroll tube, sealed with wax that crumbled at his touch.

Inside was the original testimony—a servant's account that clearly named the nephew as the poisoner, complete with the magistrate's own notation: *Testimony suppressed. Payment received: forty taels of silver.*

Chen wept as he read it. He would announce the truth at dawn, clear Madame Hu's name, and give her spirit peace.

He turned to tell her.

The old woman stood directly behind him, close enough that he should have felt her breath—but there was no breath, only cold.

"You found it," she said.

"Yes, old mother. Tomorrow, I will—"

"No."

Her hand, gray as ash, closed around his wrist. Her grip was ice and iron.

"Every magistrate who found the truth tried to wait until morning. And something always stopped them. A sudden illness. A fire. An accident on the stairs. Sixty years of accidents."

Chen tried to pull away but could not move.

"The nephew lived to old age," she continued. "He had sons. His sons had sons. They hold power in the capital now. They have protected this secret across three generations, though they have forgotten why. The corruption has become the family's very blood."

"Then what would you have me do?" Chen gasped.

"Speak the truth now. Not tomorrow. Now. Go into the street and shout it to the night. Let the words exist in the air, in the ears of whoever might hear—a drunk, a beggar, a dog. It does not matter. Just speak it before they stop you."

"They? Who—"

The lantern flickered.

In its guttering light, Chen saw them: shadows gathering in the doorway, shapes that had once been men but were now only hunger and silence. The nephew's agents, those who had carried out his family's dark work across the decades. They had died in that service, and death had not released them from it.

"Choose," said Madame Hu. "Run and speak, or stay and join them."

---

Chen ran.

He burst from the yamen into the moonless street, scroll clutched to his chest, and he screamed the truth to the empty air—the nephew's name, the bribed magistrate's name, the murdered woman's innocence—until his voice cracked and broke.

When the servants found him at dawn, he was sitting in the middle of the street, white-haired though he had been black-haired the night before, the scroll still in his hands.

He never spoke of what he had seen in the hours between his shouting and the sunrise. But he published the old testimony, sent copies to the capital, and though the powerful family tried to suppress it, the truth had already escaped into the world. It passed from mouth to mouth, as truths do, impossible to fully silence.

---

They say that Madame Hu's ghost was never seen again in Qinghe.

But Chen Weiming, who lived thirty more years and was remembered as the most just magistrate in the district's history, kept a single paper lantern burning in the Hall of Records every night until he died.

When asked why, he would only say: "Some lights should not be allowed to go out."

And if travelers passing the old yamen on autumn nights sometimes saw a faint glow in the windows and heard a woman's voice, soft and distant, saying *thank you, thank you*—well.

That is only a story.

Isn't it?
